A group of men seated on the ground in the shade of a tree. Second from left is an elder, identified as Ubang-wi-Nyidoor, a nobleman who had his 'court' at Pinythin on the Akobo river. He was the acknowledged leader of the Ulueth lineage and as such had power over a number of villages in eastern Anuakland.

A section of vegetation or gardens, possibly including a planted ?fruit tree, with a homestead in the background. Judging by the original film number there is the possibility that this is part of Pirgwinyo village in eastern Anuakland.

Two expedition carriers washing in a wide, shallow stretch of the Akobo river near Nyighum village. Evans-Pritchard notes that the expedition made its way down the Akobo towards his base at Pochala during March 1935.

Two expedition carriers washing in a wide, shallow stretch of the Akobo river near Nyighum village. Evans-Pritchard notes that the expedition made its way down the Akobo towards his base at Pochala during March 1935.

A view of the sparsely grassed savannah with trees and shrubs beyond, possibly near Pochala. Since Evans-Pritchard was in Anuakland during March-May this image shows the savannah at the beginning of the rainy season.

A view of sparse savannah vegetation with the huts of a village beyond, possibly just beyond a dried river-bed (darker colour), possibly Pochala or near Pochala?. Since Evans-Pritchard was in Anuakland during March-May this image shows the savannah at the beginning of the rainy season.

A wide section of the Oboth river in western Anuakland with vegetation either side of it.

A portrait of a carrier with baggage on the ground during a break in the day's march across Anuakland. Evans-Pritchard notes that he was able to recruit Anuak porters locally in Akobo at the beginning of the two month expedition in March 1935.

Two carriers with baggage on the ground during a break in the day's march across Anuakland. The man on the left is Oyo, Evans-Pritchard's Anuak servant and occasional translater. Evans-Pritchard notes that he was able to recruit Anuak porters locally in Akobo at the beginning of the two month expedition in March 1935.

A carrier walking past baggage (including a rifle and shotgun) laid on the ground during a break in the day's march across Anuakland. Evans-Pritchard notes that he was able to recruit Anuak porters locally in Akobo at the beginning of the two month expedition in March 1935.

A carrier walking past baggage (including a rifle and shotgun) laid on the ground during a break in the day's march across Anuakland. Evans-Pritchard notes that he was able to recruit Anuak porters locally in Akobo at the beginning of the two month expedition in March 1935.
A full length portrait of a man on a path wearing a length of fringed textile near Ugak village in western Anuakland. This man was possibly the headman of Ugak, namely Ogut-wa-Giilo.

A woman with a gourd vessel on her head and two men, one an elder and the other with a hunting rifle over his shoulder, photographed during the expedition's march along the Akobo river to Pochala. This village was the clan centre of the important Jowatcuaa clan (named after it's lineage founder, Ocala) although it had no headman but prominent clan elders.

Three young women, one carrying a gourd vessel, another with a carrying ring on her head, wearing bead-fringed skirts. This village was the clan centre of the important Jowatcuaa clan (named after it's lineage founder, Ocala) although it had no headman but prominent clan elders.

A large and sacred Tamarind tree, located to the west of Pochala near some falls on the Akobo river. This sacred tree was known as "Aboori" after a woman who was buried (wrapped in mats and thornwood) in its branches.
A portrait of a seated young man with other youths craning their necks to see the camera, under the shelter of a large canvas tent put up by Evans-Pritchard at Pochala.

A large and sacred Tamarind tree (with a ?Sycamore to the right), located to the west of Pochala near some falls on the Akobo river. This sacred tree was known as "Aboori" after a woman who was buried (wrapped in mats and thornwood) in its branches.

The huts of Dibango village seen from a distance over a stretch of dry cracked earth. Around the village is a derelict stockade of branches stuck in the ground, and in front of that a shallow ditch or moat, erected in the past as a form of defence against raids.

A fenced grave of a commoner situated within a homestead adjacent to a hut. Anuak commoners are buried in a shaft dug in the homestead, with a fence erected around it, the grave itself being kept clean and smoothed with sand.

Large tufts of grass leading up to a derelict stockade of branches stuck in the ground surrounding the huts of Dibango village, and in front of that a shallow ditch or moat, constructed in the past as a form of defence against raids.
A woman in Pochala village sweeping clean her compound floor with a stiff grass brush. Behind her is a thatched hut with low eaves and a grass fence.
A woman in Pochala village sweeping clean her compound floor with a stiff grass brush. Behind her is a thatched hut with low eaves and a grass fence.

A large and sacred Tamarind tree (with a ?Sycamore to the right), located to the west of Pochala near some falls on the Akobo river. This sacred tree was known as "Aboori" after a woman who was buried (wrapped in mats and thornwood) in its branches.

A thatched grave-hut (duat) of a man from a noble lineage (identified as Cam-wa-Medho of the Jowatcuaa clan) surrounded by a fence stockade, located close to the village of Dibango. Nobles were buried on a platform in a deep shaft, with another platform above and a hut constructed over the top and the entrance sealed. Finally, a stockade is built around the hut. Such graves are shown respect when people pass by through removing sandals and other observances.

A group of carriers in the distance resting during a break in the day's march across Anuakland. Evans-Pritchard notes that he was able to recruit Anuak porters locally in Akobo at the beginning of the two month expedition in March 1935. This sort of grassy plain is characteristic of western Anuakland south of Akobo as far as Utalo on the Oboth and Nyighum on the Akobo, and may have been taken during his march back to Akobo in May 1935.
Looking along the path ahead through grass savannah a woman carries a gourd vessel on her head, possibly returning from a pool or well nearby.
Looking along the path ahead through grass savannah a woman carries a gourd vessel on her head, possibly returning from a pool or well nearby.

A homestead with a granary seen from a distance in or near the village of Pochala. Evans-Pritchard estimated the village to have a population of between 500-1000 in 1935, and although being the main settlement of the significant Jowatcuaa clan, it had no headman of its own.

A woman sitting on the ground weaving a cylindrical piece of basketry, with a gourd of water for wetting the grass strips next to her. Another woman is preparing flour behind a tall reed screen nearby, and a group of children look on. The whole group are laughing.
A homestead with a granary to the left and other huts seen from a distance in open country. Several trees and garden crops can be seen growing around the homestead.
A homestead with a granary to the left and other huts seen from a distance in open country. Several trees and garden crops can be seen growing around the homestead.

In the distance across the grassy plain can be seen a bank of raised ground and a line of Balanites Aegyptiaca (date) trees, the site of the royal village Umar, a residence of the younger wives of past Anuak kings without children. Oko village was where royal wives with children resided.
A hut with low eaves within a homestead, with bundles of thatching grass and a pole with objects hanging from it to the right.

Hut roofs of the village of Ugak seen from a distance across a open area of fields. Predominantly agriculturalists, the Anuak clear the fields (often in forest soil) sometime around March and April and sow in May as the rains come on. Since Evans-Pritchard was in Anuakland during this part of the year only it is likely that this field has just been cleared of vegetation ready for sowing.

A small domed hut with a low entrance and a short section of fence behind, identified as a dry-season camp (location unknown). For villages situated at the edge of the wet season flood extent such as the districts of Ciro, Oyuaa, and Adongo along the Oboth, and Nyikaani district of the Akobo, it was often necessarily to move in the drought to locations closer to the river for fishing and everyday water needs. Since Evans-Pritchard was in Anuakland during the drought he was able to photograph shelters used during this time of the year.

A man wearing a long textile body cloth, walking through long grass, identified as a nobleman of Digiira village, an area under the influence of the Nyigoc lineage. Evans-Pritchard identifies one of two nobles living in this village, namely Agaanya-war-Uliimi.

A man wearing a long textile body cloth, walking through long grass, identified as a nobleman of Digiira village, an area under the influence of the Nyigoc lineage. Evans-Pritchard identifies one of two nobles living in this village, namely Agaanya-war-Uliimi.

A portrait of a seated man (identified as King Aguaa-war-Akuon of Obuodhi village) sitting on a stool with another royal stool beside him and a leopard skin laid out in front. He is wearing the royal strings of beads, which are used to invest all new Anuak kings, and are identified with the founder of the nobles lineage. The royal spear-rest holding a spear can also be seen to the right.

A group of men and three nobles seated on the ground at Kinha village (associated with the Jowatong clan). The nobles are sitting on a floor cloth due to their status, identified from the left as Abula-wa-Gilo (smoking water pipe), Anyoonya-wa-Thomo and Por-wa-Ngeenyo. Abula is noted as a noble of Kinha village, with Anyoonya residing at Udhak.

Two forked posts and a carved fence support (dikweri) indicate that this entrance way to a homestead is that of one of the nobles of Ukaadi, possibly the leading noble Akwei-war-Alal. Near the entrance is a tree with a thick trunk, probably a shaded seating area known as wic mac. In western and other Anuak districts, such symbols as dikweri adorn the compound of a headman.

An expedition porter pulling a bullet from his cartridge belt, a rifle on the ground next to him. It was usual on such long expedition marches to shoot game to feed the group of carriers as well as to present to local people as gifts.

A view of a treeless floodplain during the expedition march. This sort of grassy plain is characteristic of western Anuakland south of Akobo as far as Utalo on the Oboth and Nyighum on the Akobo, and may have been taken during his march back to Akobo in May 1935.

A view of grass savannah and scattered trees, characteristic of parts of western Anuakland south of Akobo as far as Utalo on the Oboth and Nyighum on the Akobo. The photo may have been taken during his march back to Akobo in May 1935 along the Oboth river.

A view of grass savannah and scattered trees, characteristic of parts of western Anuakland south of Akobo as far as Utalo on the Oboth and Nyighum on the Akobo. The photo may have been taken during his march back to Akobo in May 1935 along the Oboth river.

A view across a compound with huts and small children in Ukaadi village, towards a small fence plastered with mud and decorated with waving lines ornamented on the top with a fringe of grass tufts. The base of the courtyard fence is also decorated in a similar manner. It is probable that the small decorated fence was to the prevent occupants within the courtyard from being visible through the adjacent entrance way.

A girl in Pochala village bending down showing a handful of flour from a gourd vessel, with a long wooden pestle to pound grain (probably millet) in a sunken mortar next to her. A grass brush for keeping the area around the mortar clean is nearby.

A girl in Pochala village bending down showing a handful of flour from a gourd vessel, with a long wooden pestle to pound grain (probably millet) in a sunken mortar next to her. A grass brush for keeping the area around the mortar clean is nearby.

A group of youths seated on the ground around a nobleman (identified as Cam-war-Akwei) who is sitting on an antelope skin, wrapped in a textile with a European hat. This Cam-war-Akwei was one of three so-named sons of Akwei-wa-Cam, one of the most powerful nobles of the preceeding generation who lived at Utalo, and was head of a noble lineage. His brother, also called Cam, held the royal emblems from 1921-27 but died in colonial captivity in 1933.

Two men hoeing in a seated position with sticks in a field near Pochala village. Predominantly agriculturalists, the Anuak clear the fields (often in forest soil) sometime around March and April and sow in May as the rains come on. Since Evans-Pritchard was in Anuakland during this part of the year only, this indicates that this cleared field is being sown in early May.
A view through trees towards the expanse of flood water known as Oleng on the Akobo river south of Pochala.

A group of carriers in the distance during a march across Anuakland savannah towards Pocama, presumably heading towards Akobo. This sort of sparsely wooded plain is characteristic of western Anuakland in Adongo district, and may have been taken during his march back to Akobo in May 1935.
A close-up of a woman in Pochala village smoothing the outside of a coil-technique clay bowl before firing. A gourd container sits nearby, and another woman is visible beyond.
